title: Theosophy & the Occult Revival
summary: The late-19th-century rebirth of Western esotericism — a claimed ancient wisdom behind all religions, hidden Masters, and a magical order that fused Kabbalah and tarot into a system of the soul. Blavatsky and the Theosophical Society, the Secret Doctrine and the root races, the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, Crowley's Thelema, and Steiner; a symbology section on the tarot mapped onto the Tree of Life and the Hermetic 'as above, so below' — reckoning honestly with the fraudulent Mahatma letters, the invented pedigrees, and the dark later misuse of the root-race doctrine.
text: The late-nineteenth-century rebirth of Western esotericism — a claimed ancient wisdom behind all religions, hidden Masters in the Himalayas, a magical order that fused Kabbalah and tarot into a system of the soul, and a self-styled prophet who called himself the Beast — and the honest reckoning with its fabrications, its enormous influence on the modern world, and the dark uses to which some of its ideas were later put. The letters from the Masters In the 1870s and 1880s, a stout, chain-smoking Russian émigré named Helena Petrovna Blavatsky became the center of a sensation. Letters, she said, arrived from her hidden teachers — the Mahatmas or Masters , adepts of a secret brotherhood dwelling beyond the Himalayas — and these letters did not come by post: they materialized , dropping from the ceiling, appearing inside sealed rooms. Through them, Blavatsky claimed to transmit the Secret Doctrine , the single ancient wisdom lying behind every religion the world had ever known. In 1875, in New York, she and Colonel Henry Steel Olcott founded the Theosophical Society to spread it, later moving its headquarters to Adyar , in India. In 1885 the Society for Psychical Research sent the young investigator Richard Hodgson to India; his report concluded that the Mahatma letters were written by Blavatsky herself, passed through a sliding panel behind a "shrine" cabinet, and branded her "one of the most accomplished, ingenious, and interesting impostors in history." (The SPR formally distanced itself from that verdict a century later, in 1986, judging Hodgson's own method flawed — but no positive proof of the Masters ever emerged.) Both halves of the story are true, and both matter: Theosophy was built on claims that do not survive scrutiny, and it became, all the same, one of the most influential religious currents of the modern West. What Theosophy is Theosophy — "divine wisdom" — is the system Blavatsky set out in her two vast books, Isis Unveiled (1877) and The Secret Doctrine (1888): a grand synthesis of Eastern religion and Western occultism, claiming that all faiths are corrupted fragments of one original, secret wisdom-tradition preserved by hidden adepts. From the East it took karma and reincarnation , cosmic cycles, and spiritual evolution; from the West, Hermeticism, Neoplatonism, and Kabbalah. More than any other single movement, Theosophy introduced Hindu and Buddhist ideas to the Western public , gave the English language much of its spiritual vocabulary, and set the template for everything later called "spiritual but not religious." The doctrine of the Secret Doctrine Theosophy taught a colossal cosmic evolution. The universe and humanity develop through immense cycles of " rounds " and seven " root races ," each rising and falling, some on now-lost continents — Lemuria and Atlantis . Behind the visible world lay hierarchies of planes and beings, crowned by the Masters , the " Great White Brotherhood " of perfected adepts silently guiding human evolution. The individual soul reincarnates, bound by karma, climbing across many lifetimes toward reunion with the divine. It was a sweeping, syncretic myth of everything — and one element must be…

title: Wicca & Modern Paganism
summary: The 20th-century rebirth of Pagan religion — a nature faith of Goddess and Horned God, coven and sabbat, magic and moon. Gerald Gardner and the (false) claim of an ancient surviving witch-cult; the honest origins in ceremonial magic, Romanticism, and folk custom; the Wheel of the Year and the Wiccan Rede; the wider revival (Druidry, Heathenry, the Goddess movement); and a symbology of the pentacle and the Book of Shadows — told as a real, living modern religion that need not be old to be genuine.
text: The twentieth-century rebirth of Pagan religion in the West — a nature faith of Goddess and God, coven and sabbat, magic and moon — told honestly as what it is: not the ancient survival its founders claimed, but a real, living, modern religion assembled in living memory, and none the less genuine for it. The man who said the witches were real In 1951, England repealed the last of its Witchcraft Acts , and within a few years a retired British colonial civil servant and amateur folklorist named Gerald Gardner stepped forward with an astonishing claim. He said that witchcraft had never died — that a secret, ancient, pre-Christian religion of the Goddess had survived in hidden covens through all the centuries of persecution, and that he had himself been initiated into one, the New Forest coven, in 1939. He had trailed the idea first in a novel, High Magic's Aid (1949), then stated it outright in Witchcraft Today (1954) — carrying a preface by the Egyptologist Margaret Murray , whose theory of a surviving witch-cult it leaned on — and The Meaning of Witchcraft (1959). Through his books, his television appearances, and a witchcraft museum on the Isle of Man, Gardner launched Wicca upon the world. Almost none of the historical claim was true. There was no unbroken ancient witch-religion; the covens Gardner described cannot be traced before him; and Murray's pan-European witch-cult, as the witch-trials chapter (32) showed, is thoroughly discredited . And yet Wicca is entirely real: a new religion , sincerely believed and now practiced by hundreds of thousands, assembled in the twentieth century from older parts. Both halves of that sentence are the honest story. What Wicca is Wicca is a modern, initiatory, nature-centered Pagan religion. Most Wiccans worship a duality of the divine — a Goddess , often the Triple Goddess of maiden, mother, and crone, linked to the moon; and a Horned God of the wild, the hunt, and the turning cycle of life, death, and rebirth, linked to the sun. Divinity is felt as immanent in the natural world rather than ruling it from outside. Wiccans practice magic — understood as the focusing of will and intention — work in small groups called covens (traditionally led by a High Priestess ) or as solitaries, and hold to a simple ethic, the Wiccan Rede : " An it harm none, do what ye will ," often paired with the Law of Threefold Return , the belief that what one sends out comes back multiplied. Gardner, Valiente, and the making of a liturgy Gardner did not work alone, and the religion's literary soul was largely the work of a woman he initiated in 1953: Doreen Valiente . Becoming his High Priestess, she found his ritual book — the Book of Shadows — heavily borrowed from Aleister Crowley (Chapter 37) and other modern sources, and from 1954 she systematically rewrote it , stripping out much of the Crowley material and replacing it with luminous verse of her own. Her rewritten Charge of the Goddess — itself reworked from Crowley and from Charles Leland's Aradia — became Wicca's central devotional text, and her poetry gave the Craft the nature-mystical voice by which it is now known. title: Satanism
summary: Two completely different things wearing the same frightening name: the imaginary Devil-cult that persecutors invent (the witch trials, the blood-libel, the 1980s Satanic Panic — investigated and found baseless) and the real, mostly atheistic philosophy people actually choose. LaVey's Church of Satan and the Satanic Bible (Satan as symbol, not deity), The Satanic Temple's non-theistic church-state activism, and the small theistic fringe; a symbology of the inverted pentagram, Lévi's Baphomet, and the largely-literary Black Mass — described with the same rigor as any tradition and none of the shock.
text: Two completely different things wear the same frightening name — the imaginary Devil-cult that persecutors have invented for a thousand years, and the real, mostly atheistic philosophies that modern people have deliberately chosen — and telling them apart, with the same descriptive rigor this book gives every tradition and none of the shock, is the whole task of the chapter. The panic that found nothing Through the 1980s and into the 1990s, a wave of terror swept the United States and beyond: the conviction that a vast, hidden network of Satanists was ritually abusing and murdering children in secret. Day-care workers were accused, tried, and imprisoned on the testimony of coached children; talk shows and self-styled experts described underground cults of unimaginable evil; families were destroyed. It was called the Satanic Panic . And when the FBI's own investigator, Kenneth Lanning , examined the claims exhaustively — publishing his report in 1992, after a decade of allegations of thousands of murders — he found essentially no evidence that any of it was real. There was no network, no ritual murder, no secret Satanic conspiracy. There were only frightened people and an old, old fantasy. That is the necessary starting point, because it is the pattern of one whole side of this subject: the imagined Satanist is a scapegoat, not a believer — and has been for a very long time. Two Satanisms Everything written under the word "Satanism" falls into one of two utterly different categories, and confusing them is the source of nearly all the nonsense told about it. The first is accusatory, imaginary Satanism — the Devil-worshipping conspiracy that other people invent and project onto their enemies. It is the fabricated witches' sabbath of Chapter 32, the medieval blood-libel , the fin-de-siècle rumor of the Black Mass , and the 1980s Satanic Panic . It has almost no members, because almost no one actually belongs to it; it is a mask persecutors hang on the faces of the feared. The second is self-identified Satanism — real, living people and organizations who deliberately take the name of Satan for themselves. And here is the fact that dissolves most of the horror: the largest of them are atheists . They do not worship the Devil. They have adopted Satan as a symbol . (A smaller current, as we will see, does treat a dark god as real — but as a path of self-deification, not the child-murdering cult of the panics.) Before the modern: the one black mass that (almost) was The accusatory fantasy has, across all its centuries, exactly one well-documented near-exception, and it is worth naming precisely because it is so rare. In the Affair of the Poisons (1677–1682) at the court of Louis XIV, the Paris fortune-teller and poisoner Catherine Monvoisin, "La Voisin," ran a network selling poisons, abortions, and love-magic to the aristocracy — and, the investigation charged, arranging messes noires , "black masses" said over a naked woman's body by corrupt priests, to petition dark powers on a client's behalf. title: African Diaspora Religions
summary: The living Afro-Atlantic faiths that grew from the African religions carried into slavery — Haitian Vodou, Cuban Santería, Brazilian Candomblé, and the newer fire of Rastafari. From the oath at Bois Caïman and the Haitian Revolution, through the lwa and orichas doubled behind Catholic saints, possession and drumming, to Haile Selassie, Babylon and Zion; a symbology of the vèvè, the bead-codes, the calling drums, and concealment itself — seeing them as the rich, healing, community faiths they are, behind the racist 'voodoo' caricature. Completes the story begun in African Traditional Religion and closes the Modern age.
text: The living Afro-Atlantic faiths — Haitian Vodou, Cuban Santería, Brazilian Candomblé, Kongo-derived Palo, the Voodoo of New Orleans, and the newer fire of Rastafari — that grew from the African religions carried into slavery and reforged in the Americas, and the honest work of seeing them as the rich, healing, community faiths they are, behind the racist caricature the word "voodoo" has draped over them. The oath at Bois Caïman On a night in August 1791, in a wooded clearing called Bois Caïman in the north of the French colony of Saint-Domingue, enslaved Africans gathered around a Vodou priest, Dutty Boukman, and a priestess. A black pig was sacrificed; an oath was sworn; the spirits were called. Within days the northern plantations were in flames, and there had begun the only slave revolution in history to succeed — the thirteen-year struggle that would destroy French rule and, in 1804, create Haiti , the first Black republic. Whatever the exact details of that night — and they are debated — its meaning is not in doubt: the religion the enslaved had carried across the ocean was not a private consolation but a force that helped break their chains. This chapter is about that religion and its sisters — the faiths that survived the Middle Passage and became, in the Americas, living traditions of many millions. What the diaspora religions are These are the Afro-Atlantic religions — the descendants of the West and Central African traditions of Chapter 33, transplanted by the transatlantic slave trade and reforged in the Americas through a syncretism with Roman Catholicism (and, later, with Spiritism and Indigenous elements). Denied their gods, the enslaved hid them behind the Catholic saints and kept the essentials alive: the spirits, the ancestors, divination, initiation, drumming, and above all spirit possession . The concealment was itself a survival strategy — a whole theology worn under the mask of the master's religion. From it came Haitian Vodou , Cuban Santería and Palo , Brazilian Candomblé and Umbanda , the Voodoo and Hoodoo of Louisiana — and, in the twentieth century, the new Jamaican faith of Rastafari . Haitian Vodou Vodou centers on the lwa — the spirits, most bearing the names of old African (chiefly Fon and Yoruba) divinities and doubled with Catholic saints. Above them is the remote creator, Bondye (from the French bon Dieu ), too distant to petition directly; the ancestral homeland and cosmic source is Ginen , mythic Africa beneath the waters. The lwa are grouped into "nations," chiefly the cool, sweet-tempered Rada (African-derived) and the hot, fierce Petwo (born in the New World, out of the rage and rupture of slavery itself). Papa Legba , keeper of the crossroads, must open the gate before any other can be reached; Damballa the serpent, the love-spirit Ezili , the warrior Ogou , and the ribald graveyard Gede under Baron Samedi each have their character, colors, foods, and songs. Worship is led by a houngan or mambo in the temple ( ounfò ), around its central post, the poto mitan , down which the spirits descend; its central act is possession : through drumming and dance a lwa "mounts" a devotee — the " horse " — and speaks…

title: The Paleolithic
summary: The deepest reach of the human religious imagination — forty thousand years of painted caves, carved goddesses, deliberate graves, and a lion-headed man who never walked the earth. The Lion Man and the birth of the sacred imagination; cave art (Chauvet, Lascaux) and the shamanism debate; the Venus figurines and the contested 'goddess'; deliberate burial and red ochre; the Neanderthal question; and a symbology of the therianthrope, the hand-print, and the resonant cave — the era of maximum uncertainty, where we hold the artifacts but not the minds. Written last, it stands first.
text: The deepest reach of the human religious imagination — tens of thousands of years of painted caves, carved figures, bone flutes, deliberate graves, and a lion-headed man who never walked the earth — and the discipline of saying honestly, across so vast a silence, what the evidence can and cannot tell us about the first faith. The lion-headed man In a cave in the Swabian hills of southern Germany, some forty thousand years ago, someone took a mammoth tusk and spent an estimated four hundred hours carving it into a standing figure with the body of a man and the head of a cave lion . The Lion Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel is among the oldest known works of figurative art in the world — and its subject is a being that has never existed. To make it, its carver had to hold in mind a creature that was not in the world but in the imagination: a fusion of human and animal, a thing of another order. That single object tells us something momentous about its maker's mind — that it could imagine the unreal, the more-than-human, the sacred. It is as close as we can come to watching religion being born. What we can and cannot know This is the first chapter in time and among the last this book was able to write, and for a reason: the Paleolithic is the era of maximum uncertainty . There are no texts, no recorded myths, no informants — only objects, bones, and painted walls, tens of thousands of years old, from which we try to read a mind. The temptation to over-read is enormous, and the history of the subject is littered with confident interpretations later abandoned. So the honesty that governs this whole book governs this chapter most of all, and it will not be padded: we possess the artifacts of Paleolithic religion; we do not possess its meaning, and much of what is written about it is inference wearing the costume of fact. What the evidence is Four kinds of trace suggest that the people of the Old Stone Age had something we would recognize as religion. Deliberate burial. From at least 100,000 years ago, anatomically modern humans buried their dead on purpose, sometimes with ritual care: at Qafzeh and Skhul in Israel, bodies were laid out with pieces of red ochre and, in one case, deer antlers placed in the arms. Far later, the extraordinary graves at Sungir in Russia (c. 34,000 years old) held bodies — including two children — covered in thousands of painstakingly carved ivory beads, with spears of straightened mammoth tusk. To provision the dead is to imagine that death is not simply the end. Cave art. Deep in the caves of France and Spain — Chauvet (c. 36,000 years old), Lascaux , Altamira — Ice Age people painted horses, lions, bison, and aurochs with astonishing skill, often far inside inaccessible chambers, in the dark, where no one lived. Human figures are rare; hand-prints are common; and a few haunting therianthropes — half-human, half-animal, like the "Sorcerer" of Trois-Frères — stare out of the walls. Portable art and music. title: The Neolithic
summary: The age when humans settled, farmed, and raised the first monuments to the sacred. Göbekli Tepe — a temple built by hunter-gatherers before agriculture, overturning the old story; Çatalhöyük and the sacred in the home, with the dead beneath the floor; the megaliths (Stonehenge, Newgrange) aligned to the solstice sun; and the famous, contested Mother Goddess hypothesis, reported honestly as largely rejected by mainstream archaeology. A symbology of the T-pillar, the sky-aligned tomb, and the plastered skull — a religion we can read only in stone, never in words. Completes the Nine Ages.
text: The age when humans settled, farmed, and raised the first monuments to the sacred — a hilltop sanctuary older than agriculture, towns that buried their dead beneath the floor and kept their plastered skulls, and the great stones aligned to the turning sun — and the honest reckoning with a religion we can read only in architecture, never in words. The temple that came first On a barren hill in southeastern Turkey called Göbekli Tepe , archaeologists uncovered something that rewrote the story of religion. Rings of massive T-shaped limestone pillars , some sixteen feet tall and weighing tons, carved with foxes, snakes, boars, scorpions, and vultures, raised in great enclosures — and dated to around 9600 BCE , more than six thousand years before Stonehenge, before pottery, before writing, and, most astonishingly, at the very dawn of farming . Göbekli Tepe was built by people still largely living as hunter-gatherers . Its excavator, Klaus Schmidt, drew a revolutionary conclusion: that the old assumption — first agriculture, then surplus, then temples — might be exactly backward. Perhaps the need to gather in great numbers for ritual was itself one of the forces that drove people to settle and farm. First the temple, then the city. We now know Göbekli Tepe was not alone. Across the same region — the " Taş Tepeler ," the Stone Hills — sister sites are emerging, above all Karahan Tepe , with its own T-pillars and a startling chamber of carved phalluses and a watching human head. And the picture has grown more complex: the archaeologist E. B. Banning has argued that people may have lived at Göbekli Tepe after all, blurring the neat line between "temple" and "settlement," and the enclosures were deliberately backfilled and rebuilt over centuries. The "temple before the city" remains a powerful, genuinely revolutionary idea — and a debated one. The Neolithic revolution The Neolithic , the New Stone Age (roughly 10,000 to 3500 BCE in the Near East, later elsewhere), was the deepest transformation in human history before the modern age: the shift from wandering and hunting to farming, herding, and settled village life . It remade everything — diet, property, population, the shape of society — and it remade religion too, giving it, for the first time, permanent architecture : shrines, tombs, and monuments that stood in one place and gathered a community around the dead and the divine. We still cannot read its beliefs, for it left no writing. But for the first time, we can walk through its sacred spaces. The cult of the skull One practice binds the early Neolithic Near East together and speaks, more clearly than almost anything else, of an ancestor cult . At Jericho — one of the world's oldest towns — and across the Levant at sites like 'Ain Ghazal and Tell Ramad, people of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic (c. 9000–7000 BCE) practiced a startling rite: they buried their dead, then later dug up the skulls , modeled the faces back onto them in plaster , set shells or paint in the eye-sockets, and kept these plastered skulls among the living.
